procedural_history.originating_court: Additional Sessions Judge, First Court, Nadia (inferred from text)
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated the 17th January, 1982 of the Calcutta High Court in Criminal Appeal No. 160 of 1977, which confirmed the conviction of the appellant for an offence under Sec. 302 IPC and sentence imprisonment for life imposed by the learned Additional Sessions Judge.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: Appellant Gopinath Ghosh and two co-accused preferred Criminal Appeal No. 160 of 1977 in the Calcutta High Court. A Division Bench of the High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence imposed by the Additional Sessions Judge.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: Gopinath Ghosh appealed to the Supreme Court by Special Leave. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, set aside the conviction and sentence, and remitted the case to the learned Magistrate for disposal according to law. The Supreme Court also framed an issue for determination on March 11, 1983.

directions: The case is remitted to learned Magistrate for disposal according to law.

issue.issue_text: Whether the trial of the appellant was without jurisdiction and vitiated because he was a juvenile delinquent on the date of the offense, and therefore, the Magistrate could not have committed his case to the Court of Session.

facts: The appellant was convicted of murder by a Court of Session and sentenced to life imprisonment.
For the first time before the Supreme Court, the appellant argued that his trial was invalid because he was a juvenile at the time of the offense.
The Supreme Court ordered the Sessions Judge to conduct an inquiry into the appellant's age.

The inquiry, based on medical and school evidence, established that the appellant was between 16 and 17 years old on the date of the offense, making him a 'child' under the West Bengal Children Act, 1959.
This factual finding on age was not challenged by the State.
law: The West Bengal Children Act, 1959, contains specific procedures for handling cases involving juvenile delinquents.
Section 25 of the Act forbids a formal 'trial' of a juvenile delinquent; only an 'inquiry' can be held.
Section 24 of the Act prohibits sentencing a juvenile to imprisonment, except under specific circumstances.
A Magistrate cannot commit a juvenile's case to a regular Court of Session for trial; the case must be handled by a juvenile court (or a court with such powers).
application: The Court accepted the factual finding that the appellant was a juvenile delinquent when the crime was committed.
Based on this fact, the Court applied the provisions of the West Bengal Children Act.
It determined that the Magistrate's action of committing the case to the Court of Session was legally incorrect.
Consequently, the entire trial conducted by the Court of Session was held to be without jurisdiction and therefore vitiated (invalidated from the start).

The Court decided to overlook the procedural issue that this point was raised for the first time at the Supreme Court level, emphasizing the beneficial and socially progressive nature of the statute designed to protect children.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court accepted the appellant's argument, holding that the entire trial was without jurisdiction and vitiated. Because the appellant was proven to be a juvenile delinquent on the date of the offense, the Magistrate could not have committed his case to the Court of Session for a regular trial. The conviction was set aside, and the case was sent back to the Magistrate to be handled in accordance with the juvenile justice law.

issue.issue_text: Whether the Supreme Court should entertain a plea based on factual averments regarding the appellant's juvenility for the first time, considering the beneficial provisions of a socially progressive statute and constitutional principles.

facts: The appellant raised a new plea for the first time before the Supreme Court.
The plea was based on factual averments that the appellant was a juvenile ('child') at the time of the offense, as defined by the West Bengal Children Act, 1959.
This issue had not been raised in the trial court or the High Court.
law: The West Bengal Children Act, 1959, is a 'socially progressive statute' with 'beneficial provisions' for juvenile delinquents.

Article 39(f) of the Constitution directs the State to create policies that ensure children are given opportunities to develop in a healthy manner and are protected against exploitation and abandonment.
application: The Court acknowledged that it is ordinarily reluctant to entertain a plea based on new factual arguments for the first time.
However, the Court was equally reluctant to let a 'technicality' (the plea being raised late) nullify the benefits of a socially progressive law.
The Court weighed the procedural rule against the substantive benefits of the Children Act and the constitutional principles of protecting children under Article 39(f).
It concluded that the underlying intent of the beneficial statute and the Constitution should not be thwarted by a technical procedural objection.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided to entertain the plea, making an exception to its usual practice. It reasoned that the importance of upholding the beneficial provisions of a socially progressive statute, supported by the constitutional mandate in Article 39(f) to protect children, outweighed the procedural technicality that the plea was being raised for the first time.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the trial of the appellant was without jurisdiction and vitiated because he was a juvenile delinquent on the date of the offense, and therefore, the Magistrate could not have committed his case to the Court of Session.
appellant_arguments: The appellant argued that he was a juvenile on the date of the offense (August 19, 1974).
Consequently, the Magistrate could not have committed his case to the Court of Session, rendering the trial without jurisdiction and invalid.
respondent_arguments: The respondent's argument is not explicitly stated in the text, but by defending the conviction, they implicitly argued that the trial was valid and conducted with proper jurisdiction.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the Supreme Court should entertain a plea based on factual averments regarding the appellant's juvenility for the first time, considering the beneficial provisions of a socially progressive statute and constitutional principles.
appellant_arguments: The appellant implicitly argued that the court should entertain the plea of juvenility for the first time to ensure the benefits of the juvenile justice statute and constitutional principles (Article 39(f)) are extended to him.
respondent_arguments: The respondent raised a technical contention that the plea of juvenility should not be entertained because it was being raised for the first time in the Supreme Court.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A technicality, such as a plea being raised for the first time before the Supreme Court, will not be allowed to thwart the benefits of a socially progressive statute intended for the welfare of children. Consequently, whenever an accused who appears to be 21 years of age or younger is brought before a Magistrate, the court has a duty to inquire into the age of the accused on the date of the offense before proceeding with the trial.
obiter: The High Court, on its administrative side, may issue necessary instructions to magistrates to handle inquiries into the age of an accused.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The entire trial of the appellant is without jurisdiction and is vitiated. The report of the Sessions Judge unquestionably established by unassailable evidence that the appellant, having been 16 to 17 years of age on the date of the occurrence, was a juvenile delinquent, and therefore the Magistrate could not have committed his case to the Court of Session. The conviction under Section 302 IPC and the sentence for imprisonment for life are unsustainable and must be set aside.
legal_tests_applied: A combined reading of the West Bengal Children Act, 1959, dictates the procedure for handling juvenile delinquents. Specifically, Section 25 forbids a 'trial' and only permits an 'inquiry' to be held. Section 24, which has an overriding effect, takes away the power of the Court to impose a sentence of imprisonment on a juvenile, except under specific circumstances.
policy_considerations: The Court is reluctant to ignore, overlook or nullify the beneficial provisions of a very socially progressive statute by taking shield behind the technicality of the contention being raised for the first time in the Supreme Court.

In view of the underlying intendment and beneficial provisions of the Act read with clause (f) of Article 39 of the Constitution, which directs state policy towards securing opportunities for children to develop in a healthy manner and be protected from exploitation, it would not be proper to allow a technical contention to thwart the benefit of the provisions.

To give effect to the letter and the spirit of such socially beneficial legislation, whenever a case is brought before a Magistrate and the accused appears to be aged 21 years or below, an inquiry must be made about the age of the accused on the date of the occurrence before proceeding with the trial.
